record.title: HALTER reports autonomous resets for long-horizon robot evaluations
record.summary: An arXiv paper introduces HALTER, a system for scoring and resetting real-robot long-horizon manipulation trials. On one Franka Panda arm, the authors report successful resets in 76% of 100 episodes across four tasks, compared with 52% for AutoEval and 65% for a motion-planning baseline; reset-verification accuracy is 91%, and operator time is 24 versus 88 minutes for manual resets. On three held-out tasks, HALTER reportedly resets 74.7% of episodes versus 1.3% for per-task reset. Results are author-reported, limited to one robot and seven tabletop tasks; one main task favors the motion-planning baseline.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On four long-horizon tabletop tasks on one Franka Panda 7-DoF arm, the authors report that HALTER reset the scene in 76% of 100 episodes, versus 52% for AutoEval and 65% for motion-planning reset.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the 100 main-task episodes, the paper reports 90% task-completion scoring accuracy, 91% reset-verification accuracy and 24 minutes of operator time, compared with 76%, 78% and 88 minutes for the reported baselines/manual-reset measure. On three held-out tasks (25 episodes each), it reports 74.7% reset success versus 1.3% for per-task reset.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The single-arm study does not establish reliable autonomous reset across robot platforms, laboratories or broader task families; the paper reports only one robot and seven tabletop tasks, and HALTER is worse than the motion-planning baseline on Pot-Cook reset success (48% versus 72%).

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of reset success, scoring, verification or operator-time values was performed.
The result is limited to one Franka arm and seven tabletop tasks; transfer across platforms and laboratories is unknown.
Pot-Cook underperforms the motion-planning baseline, and intervention/time accounting may not generalize to other workflows.

brief.importance_rationale: If reproduced, automating resets and scoring across failed states could reduce a major operator bottleneck in physical robot evaluation and make long-horizon results more repeatable. The paper reports 100 episodes across four tasks and three held-out tasks on one Franka arm, so cross-robot and multi-lab value is not established.
limitations: All results are reported by the paper authors; no independent code execution, raw episode-log review or physical rerun was performed.
Experiments use one Franka Panda arm, two tabletop scenes and seven tasks; cross-robot, cross-lab and broader task-family transfer are not established.
HALTER’s reset success on Pot-Cook is 48%, below the motion-planning baseline at 72%; performance gains are not uniform.
Held-out evaluation covers three tasks and 25 episodes per task; no broad distribution shift or task-creation result is shown.
The operator-time measure counts each human intervention as one manual reset; broader labor costs, hardware uptime and wall-clock throughput economics are not established.
brief.summary: An arXiv paper introduces HALTER, a system for scoring and resetting real-robot long-horizon manipulation trials. On one Franka Panda arm, the authors report successful resets in 76% of 100 episodes across four tasks, compared with 52% for AutoEval and 65% for a motion-planning baseline; reset-verification accuracy is 91%, and operator time is 24 versus 88 minutes for manual resets. On three held-out tasks, HALTER reportedly resets 74.7% of episodes versus 1.3% for per-task reset. Results are author-reported, limited to one robot and seven tabletop tasks; one main task favors the motion-planning baseline.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 76% reset success across 100 episodes on four tasks, 90% completion-score accuracy, 91% reset-verification accuracy, and a reduction in operator time from 88 to 24 minutes versus manual reset. The three held-out-task result is 74.7% against 1.3% for a per-task reset policy. These are author-reported measurements.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper documents its Franka-arm setup, task protocols, episode denominators, matched reset baselines and tabulated results. the research desk did not execute the code or inspect raw trial logs; measured outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: HALTER builds a time-indexed scene graph from RGB-D observations and object point clouds, then uses an LLM to score task progress, plan restoration from the observed terminal state and verify the reset. A planner composes learned atomic reset skills from a shared library instead of training a separate reset policy for each possible terminal state.
technical.regime: One Franka Panda 7-DoF arm with three RGB-D cameras. Four long-horizon tabletop tasks and three held-out tasks; 25 episodes per task. The study uses Qwen3.5-397B for scoring, reset planning and verification, learned X-VLA reset skills, and comparisons with AutoEval and a motion-planning reset.
technical.strongest_baseline: AutoEval uses one task-specific reset policy per task with the same LLM for scoring/verification; the motion-planning baseline keeps HALTER’s planner and scoring pipeline but executes fixed grasp/motion skills. For held-out tasks the comparison is against a per-task reset policy.

brief.title: HALTER reports autonomous resets for long-horizon robot evaluations
brief.why_it_matters: Physical-robot evaluation still depends on people restoring scenes between trials, which limits throughput and makes starting conditions less consistent. If HALTER’s bounded results reproduce, composable reset skills plus scene-state tracking could make long-horizon policy evaluation less operator-intensive. The study does not establish transfer across robots, labs or broader task families.
